repeats its outcome, not whether that outcome survives a changed task or
system.

Here, *robustness* means stability under declared, meaning-preserving changes
that should not alter the correct architecture result. The architect perturbs
an input encoding, seed, representation spelling, or apparatus setting while
preserving the task, then checks whether the supported result, constraint
status, and recovery behavior remain within predeclared limits. A failure
narrows the conclusion to the conditions that remained stable. A changed
prompt, representation semantics, or tool policy may instead define a
different system.

Held-out tasks support generalization within a declared design population only
when their sampling or selection represents that population and they remained
outside system and evaluator selection. A convenience holdout is merely unseen.

A new design family, toolchain, process node, organization, or decision class
creates a transfer claim and needs a new target evaluation. Performance and
calibration must be re-estimated at each level. Any untested change remains a
boundary on the evaluation claim. Cross factor families selectively, such as
workload with compiler or design with physical corner, when their interaction
is part of the architecture risk.

Once the tested envelope is clear, the benchmark question is whether its tasks,
rules, and reports make that result comparable to other complete workflows.

## Benchmark Health and Comparable Results

Benchmarks make comparisons repeatable, but they do not remove the need for
architecture judgment. Their job in this chapter is to instantiate the metric
map for a declared task, action space, and evidence depth. SPEC CPU, PARSEC, and
MLPerf became useful because they defined workloads, rules, and reporting
conventions that made results more comparable [@PARSEC;
@SPEC2017CPU; @MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. An AI-assisted architecture benchmark must define both
the design problem and the system allowed to work on it. Its score remains one
instrument inside the complete-workflow evaluation.

Existing suites form an evidence-depth progression rather than a catalog. At
functional RTL depth, VerilogEval tests the functional correctness of generated
Verilog [@VerilogEval]. RTLLM adds post-synthesis quality-of-result measures
[@RTLLM]. ArchEval records trajectories under declared simulator and harness
settings [@WangEtAl2026ArchEval]. A common physical flow adds a different check.
ChiPBench runs placement methods through one such flow [@WangEtAl2025ChiPBench].
Cross-stage and deployed evaluation deepen the evidence again. CLOSER-Bench
connects simulation, synthesis, static timing, and place-and-route results with
tool cost and recovery, while HSCO-Bench reaches FPGA-deployed SoC prototypes
on a declared platform [@ZhouEtAl2026CLOSERBench;
@TsaiEtAl2026HSCOBench]. Each step adds a distinct tool, check, cost, or claim
limit. The deepest completed stage still bounds the result, and none of these
suites alone establishes that a complete AI-assisted workflow improves an
architecture program over its credible alternative.

### Pinning the Task, Action Space, and Fidelity

A benchmark score is interpretable only when the release pins the task, allowed
actions, checks, and evidence depth. Reuse the frozen system and environment
identity in @tbl-complete-system-identity, then add these benchmark-specific
elements.

- the benchmark version, task and split identifiers, sampled architecture
  population, and development, holdout, and confirmation boundaries;
- the evaluator-owned hidden tests, information and feedback visible to the
  system, and any benchmark-specific permitted changes;
- the scoring, aggregation, failure, censoring, and repeated-submission rules;
  and
- the contamination record, refresh policy, and retirement criteria.

Evaluator-owned requirements, rejection checks, and scoring rules should be
immutable to the system under test. When modification of a constraint,
testbench, or tool script is itself part of the task, an independent
evaluator-owned check must determine whether the change remains legal.

Task selection determines what the benchmark can represent. Remove exact and
near-duplicate tasks across development and evaluation splits, preserve
distinct design families rather than many variants of one easy block, and
state the architecture population the suite is intended to sample. Keep
hidden tests and evaluator-owned holdouts for properties that should not be
optimized directly, but document their categories and failure rules well
enough that the task remains an engineering problem rather than a guessing
game.

Benchmark validity is an inference from tasks to a claim, not a property of the
score alone. Three questions make that inference concrete. Do evaluator-owned
checks measure success on the declared task? Does the score capture the claimed
architecture capability rather than syntax repair, harness familiarity, or
checker exploitation? Do the task distribution, artifacts, feedback, budgets,
and human interactions resemble the design programs to which the result is
applied? A claim-to-task map should connect each program claim to sampled
decisions, failure consequences, and evidence stages. Gaps in that map become
limits on the claim rather than hidden assumptions.

The deepest completed evaluation stage bounds the claim. Report the stage,
check identity, outcome category, cost, coverage and waiver status, and
candidate flow, then apply the check-specific scope from
@sec-feedback-verification-trust. Passing an earlier stage supports only the
claims that stage can test.

This hierarchy also shapes cost. It is often wasteful to send malformed RTL
directly into a long physical flow. A benchmark may use cheap checks before
expensive ones, but it must report which candidates reached each stage and
must not score a cheap proxy as though it were the stronger check. State
checkpoints can reduce repeated setup cost, provided both arms receive
equivalent access and the restored tool state is part of the system record.
Cached results must be keyed by the complete environment manifest, not only
the RTL hash, because a changed constraint, library, floorplan, activity file,
or tool version creates a different evaluation.

The evaluator also needs tests for its own apparatus. Seed benchmark releases
with known-good and known-bad designs, differential-test important checkers,
and inspect disagreements among simulators, formal tools, synthesis, and
physical-design stages. A checker bug or simulator exploit can make an invalid
candidate look capable. Treat benchmark and tool failures as first-class
results, correct affected scores, and version the repaired release.

### Contamination, Decay, and Retirement

RTL-Repo contributes 4,098 samples drawn from 1,361 public repositories
[@AllamShalan2024RTLRepo]. Public benchmark tasks may also overlap model
training data [@WangEtAl2025VeriContaminated]. When the training
corpus is available, exact and approximate overlap searches can identify
obvious reuse. When it is unavailable, the evaluation should state that limit
instead of claiming contamination freedom.

LiveCodeBench demonstrates how time-split tasks can reduce exposure to benchmark
material [@JainEtAl2025LiveCodeBench]. The architecture lesson is to reserve
tasks created after the evaluated model snapshot, then prevent their results
from guiding system configuration before final evaluation. The limitation is
equally important. A software-code benchmark does not exercise hardware tool
flows, physical constraints, costly simulation, or cross-layer architecture
decisions. Private held-out designs and newly constructed architecture problems
provide additional barriers, but none proves that a model has never encountered
the design or a close relative.
Private tasks can also leak through repeated evaluation. Record how often the
system, its developers, or its prompt-tuning process observed held-out scores or
diagnostic feedback; limit queries and feedback granularity; separate
development access from final evaluation; and rotate holdouts when repeated
submissions could reveal the evaluator. A private split becomes development
data when its feedback repeatedly guides configuration choices
[@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout].
Semantics-preserving variants can test sensitivity to surface form, but
renaming meaningful hardware signals or changing structure may also change the
task. Functional simulation, formal equivalence where its assumptions apply,
and stronger implementation checks determine whether an output satisfies the
task. They do not determine whether the output was memorized.

The practical response is layered. Publish known corpus overlap, separate
public development tasks from private evaluation tasks, record model and
benchmark dates, disable unreported retrieval during held-out tests, refresh
the held-out pool, detect near-duplicate tasks, and qualify conclusions by the
remaining exposure risk.

A benchmark can also decay when no training example leaked. Once a community
optimizes repeatedly against a fixed target, the score may stop measuring the
underlying capability. Computer architecture has a durable example.
SPEC omitted the `matrix300` workload from its 1992 suites because a legal
compiler optimization excessively influenced its SPEC ratio
[@SPEC1995FrequentlyAskedQuestions;
@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach, pp. 61--62].

An architecture benchmark therefore needs a lifecycle before its first score
is quoted. Version each release, retain a refresh pool, monitor whether task
success has saturated or become dominated by benchmark-specific tricks, and
publish retirement criteria. Old tasks can remain useful for regression
testing after they stop supporting comparative capability claims.

### Reporting Comparable Results

Publish per-task results before any suite summary. Normalized ratios across
positive-valued tasks with a common direction should generally use a geometric
mean, not an arithmetic mean, because the geometric mean is invariant to the
choice of common reference [@FlemingWallace1986HowNotToLie]. Invalid runs,
zeros, signed slacks, and heterogeneous raw quantities need a declared failure
policy rather than being inserted into that mean. Multi-objective architecture
outcomes may not admit one defensible aggregate. In that case, report the
constraint pass rate, per-objective results, and non-dominated sets rather than
inventing a weighted score that hides the decision.

Comparable reporting reuses the frozen identities and hashes established in
@tbl-complete-system-identity. Add the benchmark version, task and split
identifiers, seeds, budgets, stopping and failure rules, aggregation policy,
and scripts needed to regenerate the summary from raw results. Preserve enough
candidate and attempt records to investigate invalid scores without requiring
disclosure of proprietary design data. If a result depends on a private design,
process kit, or tool, name the inaccessible boundary and provide a public
validation path where feasible.

Trajectory measures can supplement those outcomes.

- best supported outcome versus total cost shows how quickly a system reaches
  useful results;
- proposals and failures by tool stage expose where it spends expensive
  evaluations;
- correction after a returned failure shows whether the next action resolves
  that failure without creating a disqualifying one;
- repeated states and repeated failure classes expose ineffective iteration;
  and
- proxy fidelity on an independently selected audit sample near the decision
  boundary shows whether the cheap screen retained and ordered the cases that
  mattered.

These are diagnostics, not evidence of reasoning. A trajectory area under the
curve requires a declared cost axis, common starting point and horizon,
directionally consistent normalization, feasible-candidate rule, and treatment
of failures, timeouts, and censored runs before two values can be compared.
Best-so-far is monotone by construction and says nothing about whether the
underlying path thrashed. Monotonic improvement is not a general requirement
in a multi-objective search. A useful exploration may temporarily regress one
quantity to reach a better region.

Benchmark health makes the ordinary comparison readable. Deliberate challenge
then asks whether that comparison remains trustworthy when assumptions,
interfaces, or checks are attacked.

## Red-Teaming the Candidate Design and Workflow

Ordinary evaluation asks how the system performs when its inputs, tools, and
checks behave as expected. Red teaming asks what happens when assumptions are
missing, inputs are hostile, feedback is misleading, or the scoring rule
permits improvement by weakening the task. The goal is not to assemble a
single “security score.” It is to expose concrete failure classes and measure
detection, interruption, correction, recovery, and residual uncertainty. The
selected tests challenge both the returned design and the workflow that
produced it, but no finite set forms a universal checklist.

This chapter keeps red teaming, fault injection, and robustness stress distinct
because they serve different test purposes. A red-team test gives a declared
adversary a specific path to an asset or authority. Evaluator-owned checks then
test whether the workflow detects an invalid design, interrupts the attack,
contains its effect, and supports recovery. A pass applies only to the tested
access and attack.

Nonmalicious fault injection creates a specified EDA or infrastructure failure,
such as a timeout, truncated report, or lost license, and records how the
workflow recovers. FATE and DESTINI provide a systems precedent for using such
faults to exercise recovery paths [@GunawiEtAl2011FATEDestini].

Robustness stress varies a meaning-preserving condition, such as a seed,
semantics-preserving representation change, or apparatus setting, without
changing the correct architecture result. A test may expose more than one
weakness, but its purpose and success condition must be declared before it
runs.

### Threat Models and Test Selection

Four jobs keep the red-team program tied to architecture work. First, challenge
the task and measurement assumptions by omitting requirements, weakening
constraints, or exploiting a proxy or checker. Second, challenge the tool and
environment path with stale reports, substituted components, unauthorized
access, and corrupted state. Third, challenge learned and conventional
components with poisoned information, triggers, and inputs that induce harmful
actions or suppress failures. Fourth, challenge end-to-end decision support by
testing whether the system accepts an invalid candidate, overspends its budget,
ignores an interruption, or fails to recover a trustworthy state. The detailed
test classes below instantiate those four jobs without claiming to exhaust the
attack surface.

Begin with a threat model. For the candidate design, identify the assets
that must be protected, the actors who can influence the design, the boundary
between trusted requirements and untrusted artifacts, the interfaces and tool
stages an attacker can reach, the changes the workflow is authorized to make,
and the consequences of hidden or incorrect behavior. For the design workflow,
repeat the exercise for models, retrieval and training data, represented
state, prompts, tool wrappers, checkers, credentials, compute and license
budgets, human review, and the final recommendation. A design backdoor and a
compromised workflow may interact, but they have different assets, attack
surfaces, trust boundaries, and containment measures.

The exact fields above are this chapter's synthesis for architecture work. They
adapt the broader systems-security practice of identifying protection needs,
trust relationships, interfaces, and consequences
[@RossEtAl2022EngineeringTrustworthySystems].

Select red-team tests by tracing each declared asset and authority through the
interfaces and attack surfaces that can affect it, then rank the tests by the
consequence of a successful attack. Each selected test should name that trace
and the evaluator-owned observation that can expose failure. Test families that
the threat model does not select remain explicit untested limits. Passing the
selected subset does not imply coverage of every row or attacker capability.

### Attack Mechanisms Across Artifacts, Learned Components, and Runtime

This book uses an operational split among three failure mechanisms because
they require different tests. Hidden or malicious behavior inserted into a
returned design remains in the RTL, firmware, microcode, configuration, or
implemented artifact after the design workflow has ended. A rare instruction,
state sequence, or input can activate it in the delivered system. Hardware
security literature calls a malicious circuit modification of this kind a
*hardware Trojan* and separates its physical form, activation mechanism, and
action [@TehranipoorKoushanfar2010HardwareTrojan]. For this evaluation, the
retained artifact and its activation path define that test target.

Malicious LUT shows why the evaluated artifact and tool stage matter. In this
controlled research construction, a malicious change remained functionally and
formally equivalent to the HDL through the FPGA design flow, then took effect
when place and route emitted the bitstream
[@KriegWolfJantsch2016MaliciousLUT]. This was a research demonstration, not a
reported production incident. Its lesson is narrower and durable. Source-level
simulation and formal checks do not establish the behavior of the delivered
artifact when a later stage can change it.

BadNets demonstrated that poisoned training data can leave
trigger-conditioned behavior in a trained network [@GuEtAl2019BadNets]. This
chapter applies that mechanism to architecture surrogates, learned checkers,
and learned routers. The evaluator presents the declared trigger and observes
whether the component proposes a harmful action, suppresses a failure, or
misreports a result. The returned design may contain the consequence, but the
trigger-conditioned mechanism remains in the workflow component.

Sleeper Agents provides a narrower proof of concept for language models. Its
constructed LLMs retained trigger-conditioned behavior after several safety
training procedures [@HubingerEtAl2024SleeperAgents]. This result is not
evidence that ordinary architecture agents are deceptive, and an
LLM-component trigger is not a hardware Trojan in a delivered artifact. It
does motivate rerunning declared trigger and near-trigger tests after
fine-tuning, adaptation, checkpoint replacement, or another component update
rather than assuming that the update removed the behavior.

Prompt injection is a separate runtime information-integrity test. Untrusted
instructions arrive through a prompt, retrieved document, source comment,
issue, or tool return without requiring trigger-conditioned learned behavior.
The evaluator observes whether the workflow separates design information from
instructions and preserves its operating limits. AgentDojo provides a precedent
for testing this mechanism in tool-using agents when untrusted tool returns
contain prompt injections [@DebenedettiEtAl2024AgentDojo]. It does not cover
architecture work; this chapter adapts only the attack structure. These
operational categories identify what to perturb and inspect. They do not claim
that every security failure falls cleanly into one exhaustive class.

### A Selected Red-Team Program

The threat model now determines which of these mechanisms deserves a concrete
test and which evaluator-owned observation can expose it. The test classes in
@tbl-red-team-program turn that choice into a reusable program. Each selected
row follows the same evaluation path. The evaluator checks whether the
workflow detects the invalid action or output, contains its effects, recovers a
trustworthy state, and reports the remaining risk and untested attack surface.

| **Test class** | **Example challenge** | **Required observations** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Requirement integrity** | Omit a requirement, introduce a contradiction, or make a costly function easy to discard | Did the system identify the conflict, ask for resolution, preserve the function, or accept an invalid design? |
| **Check integrity** | Remove a clock, weaken a constraint, alter a testbench, edit a scoring script, or exploit a simulator or parser discrepancy | Did an independent check detect the change before acceptance? |
| **Feedback integrity** | Return a stale, partial, malformed, or deliberately misleading tool report | Did the system bind the result to the correct candidate and conditions, reject the report, or act on it? |
| **Information integrity** | Place misleading instructions in retrieved documents, source comments, issue text, or tool logs | Did the workflow separate design information from instructions and preserve its operating limits? |
| **Confidentiality and authority** | Attempt unauthorized reads, writes, or external transmission involving proprietary RTL, process-design-kit or licensed-IP material, repositories, logs, credentials, or another project | Did least-privilege controls prevent or contain the access, record the attempt, revoke affected authority, and identify any exposed data? |
| **Returned-design behavior** | Remove isolation, memory protection, error detection, or a declared speculative-execution defense; insert hidden behavior activated only by a rare input or state | Did an evaluator-owned functional, formal, relational, or security check detect the changed behavior in the artifact? |
| **Learned or adapted component behavior** | Poison training or adaptation data, then present a trigger intended to make a model, surrogate, learned checker, or learned router propose a harmful action, hide a failure, or misreport a result | Did the declared trigger change the component's behavior, and did a trusted comparison path, component replacement, or independent check expose and contain the failure? |
| **Component and supply-chain integrity** | Substitute a model endpoint, binary, wrapper, container, package, process kit, library, IP block, compiler, benchmark dependency, cache, or manifest between evaluation and use | Did independent identity and provenance checks detect the change, prevent reuse of incompatible state, and identify every result that depended on the substituted component? |
| **Visible-score gaming** | Expose a declared PPA score for a block whose contract retains protection-domain isolation, while keeping the evaluator-owned isolation check hidden | Did PPA improve by weakening isolation, and did the hidden functional or relational check reject the candidate before acceptance? |
| **Operational control** | Force repeated states, timeouts, out-of-memory kills, scheduler preemption, disk or scratch failures, stale locks, truncated reports, missing corners, license-feature mismatch, excessive retries, unsafe tool actions, or incompatible checkpoint reuse | Could the run distinguish infrastructure failure from engineering result, stop within budget, contain tool access, release resources, preserve inspectable state, invalidate affected descendants, and restart safely? |
| **Shared blind spots** | Give proposal and checking paths the same wrong assumption or corrupted source | Did an independently developed check or reviewer expose the common failure? |

: **Threat-model-selected tests attack the design result and the workflow that
produced it.** Each test records acceptance of invalid output, detection,
interruption, correction, recovery cost, and what remains unresolved.
{#tbl-red-team-program tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

A useful feedback-integrity test places one blocking timing or design-rule
violation inside a long tool report whose candidate identity, conditions, and
other results are valid. The system should preserve and escalate that
violation rather than summarize the report as clean. Record whether it found
the exact violation, prevented acceptance, retained the relevant report
context, and required human review or another tool run to recover.

For every attack, predeclare the attacker access, target surface,
trusted evaluator-owned check, attack budget, and success condition. Also state the
consequence of success, what should detect or interrupt the attack, what counts
as recovery, and which related attacks remain untested. Give the two comparison
arms comparable attack opportunity rather than testing only the system expected
to fail. Pair seeded attacks with clean designs, difficult but benign inputs,
and near-miss triggers. Report trial count and diversity, attack success,
detection, containment, recovery, false alarms, unnecessary stops, clean-task
success, defense overhead, residual failures, uncertainty or an upper bound on
missed failures, untested attacker capabilities, and total recovery cost. Zero
observed failures is not a zero failure rate. With no failures in $n$
independent trials under the same declared conditions, a common approximate 95
percent upper confidence bound on the failure probability is $3/n$
[@HanleyLippmanHand1983ZeroFailures]. The
calculation applies only to the sampled failure event and trial population. It
does not cover untested attack classes, and passing one attack class does not
support a general security claim.

A concrete visible-score test can use a block whose declared contract requires
protection-domain isolation while the declared score rewards timing, power, and
area. The system receives the isolation requirement and visible PPA feedback,
but not the evaluator-owned relational or access-control check. A candidate
that gains PPA by removing or bypassing isolation must fail that hidden check.
Record the PPA change, violated property, whether rejection occurred before
acceptance, and which repair and implementation checks were rerun.

For a returned-design test, preserve the artifact and the exact rare input,
state, or sequence that exposed the behavior. For a learned-component test,
preserve the component version, trigger, surrounding context, proposed or
suppressed action, access used, and downstream artifacts. Replacing or
bypassing the component helps locate the workflow failure. It does not by
itself prove that a returned design is clean, so the artifact checks still run.
For a supply-chain test, preserve expected and observed component identities,
signatures or hashes where available, acquisition path, update event, manifest,
and the dependent caches, checkpoints, artifacts, and claims that must be
invalidated.

Inspectability is a prerequisite for these tests. Evaluator-owned or otherwise
tamper-resistant capture should connect each action to the system version,
candidate state, inputs, tool call, returned result, access decision, human
intervention, cost, and final status. Red-team attempts should try to delete,
rewrite, truncate, or selectively omit that record. When a test fails, the
evaluator must be able to determine what the system used, what it changed, and
which later results may have inherited the failure.

### Exposing Proxy Failure

Proxy qualification, including the learned-placement dispute and the scope of a
stronger physical check, belongs to
@sec-proxy-mismatch-metric-gaming-and-calibration. Complete-workflow evaluation
adds a different requirement. Adaptive search changes the candidate
distribution by concentrating queries where the proxy predicts improvement,
including regions where its errors are easiest to exploit. Even when proxy
errors average to zero before selection, choosing the best predicted candidate
preferentially selects optimistic errors. Decision analysis calls this effect
the *optimizer's curse* [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. The source does not
study EDA proxies. The architecture response is an independent,
higher-fidelity audit of the candidates selected by the search.

A static holdout is therefore insufficient. Preserve an evaluator-selected
audit stream or refreshable holdout that remains outside proxy fitting, search,
and workflow tuning. At declared search-budget points, independently sample the
selected and near-boundary candidates, send them to the higher-fidelity check,
and retain their candidate flow and check cost. Reusing only proxy-fitting or
search-selected points for this audit introduces selection bias.

Report stronger-check error as search budget grows, including uncertainty,
pairwise misranking, retention of the strongest candidates, and the
stronger-check gap between the selected and best audited candidates near the
acceptance boundary. Here, the stronger-check gap between the selected and best
audited candidates is the difference between their values under the
stronger-check objective. Also test whether support or out-of-distribution
warnings identify cases the proxy should decline. This audit measures whether
proxy qualification survives the workflow's own adaptive pressure rather than
repeating the underlying placement comparison.

### Attacking Constraints and Unrewarded Requirements

An optimizer rewarded for performance and area has an incentive to remove
anything costly that the score does not protect. The simplest attack is not a
better design. It is a weaker task.

The deleted-clock example from @sec-architecture-20-ontology makes the failure
plain. Removing a clock definition can produce a clean timing report because
the intended sequential paths are no longer analyzed. The evaluation must
confirm that required constraints were loaded and unchanged, that the
candidate still implements the declared function, and that the scoring checks
were not modified by the system they judge.

Other attacks remove error correction, memory protection, isolation, or
security mitigations because these features cost power, area, or performance.
The needed check depends on the property. Assertions and model checking can
cover selected single-execution safety properties such as permission
enforcement. Those single-execution checks are insufficient when the target is
a relational information-flow property across executions
[@ClarksonSchneider2010Hyperproperties]. For speculative execution, SPECTECTOR
uses symbolic execution to check speculative noninterference under explicit
speculative semantics [@GuarnieriEtAl2020SPECTECTOR]. This is a
property-specific example, not a requirement that every timing issue use the
same analysis. A generic “formal passed” flag is not enough.

Formal equivalence also has a boundary. It applies when candidate and reference
are intended to have the same observable behavior. Architecture changes that
alter latency, protocols, or permitted behavior need a different relation.
Refinement mappings provide a formal precedent for proving that one system
implements another at a different level of abstraction
[@AbadiLamport1991RefinementMappings]. This chapter applies that precedent as a
refinement check whose declared relation states which latency, protocol, or
behavioral changes are permitted when bare equivalence no longer applies.

Timing exceptions deserve the same treatment. Altera documents false-path and
multicycle-path constraints as exceptions that modify the default timing
analysis behavior [@Altera2026TimingExceptionConstraints]. They are assumptions,
not timing repairs. This book recommends crediting an exception only when
endpoint-specific timing intent and protocol or property checks justify it. A
structural clock-domain report or documentation alone does not settle it.

Adversarial tests challenge intent and trust boundaries. The next step removes
the adversary and injects operational faults to test interruption and recovery.

## Fault Injection, Interruption, and Recovery

Fault injection tests whether the workflow can detect a nonmalicious failure,
stop affected work, preserve inspectable state, and recover without carrying a
bad result forward. Useful tests trigger tool timeouts and process kills, queue
or scheduler interruption, partial or nominally successful but incomplete
reports, license-feature failures, scratch or database corruption, stale locks,
incompatible incremental checkpoints, missing analysis modes or corners, and
budget exhaustion. Measure time to detection, actions taken after the fault,
ability to revoke tool access, state preserved for inspection, recovery time,
repeated work, and whether the final evaluation excludes results produced after
the failure. An adversarial test may use the same mechanism when an attacker
causes or exploits the fault, but the two results should not be reported as the
same test.

Repeated-state behavior is one failure that fault injection should expose. An
unattended workflow can turn a small disagreement into a large cost. A
generator may rename a signal to fix lint, trigger equivalence failure, revert
the change, and repeat the original lint failure. Two components can continue
the cycle indefinitely if neither recognizes a repeated state and neither owns
a retry limit.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="A repeated-state loop"}
**The trap.** A proposal component and a checking component repeatedly
alternate between the same lint failure and the same equivalence failure.

**The mechanism.** Each component responds correctly to its immediate input,
but the configured technical system has no cycle detector, shared retry budget,
or stopping rule for repeated states.

**The lesson.** Evaluation must test whether the complete workflow stops,
releases tool resources, preserves the last trustworthy state, reports why it
stopped, and can resume without restoring the failed action. This is an
illustrative composite failure pattern, not one documented incident.
:::

Repeated movement is not the same as temporary regression. Constraint repair
need not improve every count monotonically. Fixing one setup path may expose a
hold path, and routing one net may create a local spacing violation. The
failure is movement among the same states without progress on the blocking
conditions. The schematic traces in @fig-whac-a-mole use synthetic counts only
to show why a recurring count should trigger state inspection.

```{python}
#| label: fig-whac-a-mole
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **A recurring violation count is a warning, not proof of a repeated design state.** The green illustrative trace burns the blocking timing and design-rule violations down. The red trace settles into a recurring count pattern after an initial improvement. These synthetic counts do not identify the candidate, constraint, violation, or tool state. A real evaluation needs those identities to establish a repeated-state cycle and should not require every useful multi-objective search to be monotonic.
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of blocking timing and design-rule violations over twenty tool iterations. A green illustrative trace declines to zero. A red dashed trace declines at first and then alternates between ten and twenty violations."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

iterations = np.arange(21)
directed = [max(0, int(value)) for value in 50 * np.exp(-0.25 * iterations)]
repeated = [
    int(50 * np.exp(-0.2 * index)) if index < 5 else 15 + 5 * (-1) ** index
    for index in iterations
]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.95, top=0.88, bottom=0.18)

ax.plot(
    iterations,
    directed,
    linewidth=2.5,
    color=COLORS["green"],
    label="Directed repair",
)
ax.plot(
    iterations,
    repeated,
    linewidth=2.0,
    linestyle="--",
    color=COLORS["red"],
    label="Recurring violation count",
)

ax.annotate(
    "inspect state identity",
    xy=(10, 20),
    xytext=(11, 31),
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["ink"], lw=0.8),
    fontsize=6,
    color=COLORS["ink"],
)

ax.set_xlabel("Tool iteration", fontsize=6.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Blocking violations", fontsize=6.5)
ax.set_xlim(0, 20)
ax.set_ylim(-2, 55)
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=6.5, loc="upper right")
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=5.9, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.55, zorder=0)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
```

Both paths reduce the initial count, but the green path continues toward zero
while the red path settles into a recurring count pattern. That sawtooth is a
warning to inspect the run, not proof that the same design state repeated.
Different candidates can have the same number of blocking violations, and the
same count can hide changes in violation type, endpoint, severity, or
constraint coverage.

Establishing a repeated state requires the candidate or artifact identity, the
loaded constraints, tool and checker versions and settings, seed, violation
identities and severities, relevant checkpoint or tool state, and the action
that led there. A cycle detector can then compare state signatures and action
history rather than treating an equal count as an equal state. The count trace
finds suspicious behavior. The preserved identities determine whether the
workflow actually revisited a state.

Correction matters as much as interruption. For each injected fault, the
architect identifies the descendant artifacts, cached results, and claims that
may be tainted, then observes whether the workflow invalidates them, restores an
approved checkpoint, contains affected authority, releases tool and license
resources, and reruns the affected checks. Conclusions remain withdrawn until
those reruns re-establish them. The architect should also check whether
corrupted retrieval entries, scripts, checkpoints, or tool state remain active.
When clean state cannot be reconstructed, the result remains unresolved.

Only after outcomes, costs, reliability, deliberate attacks, and recovery are
joined can the evaluator state what the complete workflow supports.

## Reporting What the Evaluation Supports

A complete-workflow evaluation combines results across tasks with the matched
comparison, costs, component tests, varied conditions, and attacks needed to
judge the AI-assisted system. The chapter's supporting records define the
system identity (@tbl-complete-system-identity), matched comparator
(@tbl-matched-system-comparison), metric map (@tbl-evaluation-metric-map),
component tests (@tbl-system-ablations), cost and candidate flow
(@tbl-total-system-cost; @tbl-attempt-cost-record; @tbl-candidate-funnel),
condition variation (@tbl-complete-workflow-condition-variation), and challenge
program (@tbl-red-team-program). The final assessment retains six reporting
fields while pointing to those records rather than repeating them
(@tbl-complete-system-assessment).

| **Evaluation field** | **Required content and chapter record** |
| --- | --- |
| **Frozen identity and comparator** | Name the configured system, complete workflow, task, environment, legal actions, checks, budgets, and strongest practical alternative. Record any mismatch. |
| **Architecture result** | Report each task's supported result or failure, comparator, uncertainty, deepest completed check, and explicit nonclaims. Include manufacturing, test, packaging, or bring-up evidence only when the evaluation reached those stages. |
| **Decision behavior and component contribution** | Report useful observations, supported decisions, false accepts and rejects, escalation, stopping, recovery, and human overrides. Separate the complete-workflow effect from only those component dependencies that controlled comparisons can isolate. |
| **Total cost and candidate flow** | Publish the resource classes, attempt-level costs, and per-arm candidate flow. Retain failed and censored work, and apply the no-double-counting rule. |
| **Reliability, benchmark, and challenge results** | Report repeated behavior, the tested condition envelope, benchmark version and health, and selected red-team and fault-injection results. Name untested conditions and attacks. |
| **Program claim status** | Mark the complete-workflow claim and every narrower component claim as supported, unsupported, or unresolved within the named tasks, conditions, costs, checks, and challenge coverage. |

: **The final output assembles rather than repeats the chapter's evaluation
records.** It points reviewers to the frozen comparison, architecture result,
decision behavior, costs, reliability, challenges, and resulting claim status.
{#tbl-complete-system-assessment tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

Reviewers who want to apply this assembled assessment to an external paper or
artifact package can use the optional instrument in
@sec-appendix-a-reviewer-checklist.

The three status terms need explicit rules.

**Supported.** Repeated matched comparisons across the predeclared tasks and
conditions must clear a decision boundary with their paired effect and
uncertainty. Either the architecture improvement reaches its minimum worthwhile
level within the acceptable total-cost envelope, or the cost reduction reaches
its minimum worthwhile level while architecture-quality loss stays below its
maximum acceptable level. A method, component, or AI-contribution claim also
needs a controlled comparison. Its dependencies, failures, attacks, and
uncertainty must be understood well enough to support the stated scope.

**Unsupported.** Matched comparisons with the declared task coverage and
resolving power directly contradict the claim or fail both decision tests. They
show neither the minimum worthwhile architecture improvement within the
acceptable cost envelope nor the minimum worthwhile cost reduction while
keeping architecture-quality loss below its maximum acceptable level. A
successful candidate can therefore coexist with an unsupported workflow
adoption or AI-contribution claim.

**Unresolved.** The claim remains unresolved when the credible alternative was
not run, important costs were omitted, the task set is too narrow, or a
disqualifying stage was not reached. It also remains unresolved when uncertainty
obscures the difference, a paired interval overlaps the decision boundary, or
the comparison cannot resolve the minimum worthwhile architecture improvement,
minimum worthwhile cost reduction, or maximum acceptable architecture-quality
loss. Interactions that prevent isolation of a component contribution and
red-team failures that leave the result unreadable have the same status.
Unresolved is not a polite form of supported.

Applied to @sec-running-the-loop, these rules keep the unexecuted Lighthouse
cache record separate from the executed array record and state what each
supports, what is unsupported, or what remains unresolved.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="Current records leave the Lighthouse unresolved"}
The Lighthouse cache study remains unexecuted, and the separate retained array
record does not test its architecture question.

- **Architecture result.** The array comparison remains limited to its source
  scope, as established in @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack. It supports a local
  no-change result for the evaluated set but does not test the cache question, XR
  workload, 3\ W target, or implementation-facing checks, so the Lighthouse
  result remains unresolved.
- **Workflow and decision behavior.** The array record reports a technical
  recommendation that still awaited author confirmation. It does not evaluate
  whether a complete workflow selected appropriate methods and tools, preserved
  state, interpreted returns, or escalated well, so this judgment remains
  unresolved.
- **Total cost.** The array record preserves only partial model and simulator
  costs. It omits matched total human, machine, license, review, and per-attempt
  tool cost for complete alternatives, so any cost advantage remains unresolved.
- **Reliability of the advantage.** One run under a synthetic workload and fixed
  simulator configuration cannot establish repeatability, robustness, or
  generalization and transfer across workloads, designs, tools, and operating
  conditions. Reliability remains unresolved.

The complete-workflow effect and Lighthouse moonshot remain unresolved. The
retained model-versus-fixed-heuristic comparison under equal simulator-event
budgets supports only the narrow finding that the model had no advantage over
the fixed heuristic in the evaluated array study. Matched total-cost
attribution and broader claims about component contribution remain unresolved.
These judgments identify the comparisons, costs, conditions, and attacks needed
to change those statuses.
:::

These statuses describe the evaluation evidence. They do not decide whether an
architecture advances.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Substituting a component score for an architecture result.** A good
  predictor, generator, or optimizer score can hide a blocking check, failure
  at higher fidelity, or repair cost that leaves the candidate or complete
  workflow worse.

- **Counting attempts as independent architecture tasks.** Treating retries,
  candidates, seeds, or tool calls as independent samples inflates sample size
  and confidence while hiding attrition and realized cost.

- **Training on the evaluation.** Reusing held-out, benchmark, or red-team
  feedback during development teaches the system the evaluator, so familiar
  checks pass while fresh designs, higher-fidelity stages, or new attacks fail.

## Open Questions

Evaluating an AI-assisted system requires comparable architecture
outcomes, complete cost accounting, reliable behavior, and tests that expose
how the system fails. The questions below ask how evaluation can separate
contribution, judge decisions, preserve comparability, and reveal failures that
ordinary benchmarks miss.

**Measuring contribution and total cost.** Complete workflows contain
interacting learned components, conventional tools, and human work. The value
of assistance cannot be inferred from one strong candidate or one fast local
step.

- **How can an evaluation identify which interacting components improve an
  architecture result without testing every possible combination?**
  One-at-a-time replacements miss interactions, while exhaustive tests can cost
  more than the design work being evaluated. The open problem is to identify a
  small set of component combinations whose direct comparison exposes decisive
  changes in supported architecture quality or total cost.

- **When does an AI-assisted system cease to earn its total cost as architecture
  difficulty rises?** The answer requires comparison with a credible alternative
  as design-space size, feedback latency, verification burden, or tool fidelity
  changes. Architecture quality and blocking failures must be measured alongside
  model and tool calls, simulation and physical-design runs, tokens, elapsed
  time, and human review.

**Decision quality and benchmark validity.** A final candidate reveals too
little about the decisions that produced or rejected it, and a fixed benchmark
can become easier to exploit than the capability it represents.

- **How can an evaluation distinguish a justified rejection, abstention, or
  escalation from premature stopping or unnecessary continued work?**
  Difficult cases combine plausible architecture gains with incomplete
  measurements, conflicting checks, or uncertainty that additional tool runs
  may not resolve. A useful evaluation must measure escaped failures,
  architecture quality, additional tool and review cost, and whether escalation
  changed the supported conclusion.

- **How can benchmarks for AI-assisted systems remain comparable as tasks,
  workloads, and tool flows change?** Stable anchor tasks and overlapping
  releases can reveal whether a score change comes from the system or the
  benchmark, but stale tasks eventually stop representing current architecture
  work. Comparable reports must disclose system identity, task and split
  versions, legal actions, budgets, human intervention, and material differences
  between releases.

**Reliability, security, and failure behavior.** An apparent advantage may
disappear across repeated runs, changed conditions, benign faults, attacks,
interruptions, or recovery.

- **Which stress tests best predict when an AI-assisted system will lose its
  advantage in architecture quality or total cost?** Relevant stresses include
  repeated runs, workload and tool changes, benign faults, interrupted
  execution, and evaluator-owned attacks. Their value depends on whether early
  failures predict later losses in supported architecture quality, total cost,
  failure detection, or recovery within the declared evaluation population.

- **Which red-team tests expose hidden behavior, backdoors, or checker
  exploitation that ordinary architecture benchmarks miss?** Ordinary and
  adversarially triggered runs can challenge poisoned information, weakened
  constraints, hidden RTL behavior, malicious tool returns, and triggered
  learned components. Useful tests must report attack success, detection and
  false-alarm rates, escaped architecture violations, containment, and recovery
  without treating one tested attack as evidence of general security.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Evaluate the architecture, the assistance, and their limits separately"}
Measure the returned architecture first. Separately determine whether the
complete AI-assisted workflow or a named component caused an improvement, why
it did so, what total human and machine cost it required, and whether the
advantage survives changed conditions and deliberate attacks. Do not collapse
those results into one score.
:::

Evaluation separates the candidate design, method or component, configured
technical system excluding human decision work, and complete
human-plus-technical workflow. The architecture result shows what the workflow
achieved. Coordination and decision measures show whether it selected suitable
methods and tools, preserved state, interpreted results correctly, and
escalated when needed. Total cost shows whether a local speedup survived model
use, data preparation, tools, verification, integration, review, recovery, and
future change work.

A credible comparison holds the architecture question and evaluator-owned
checks fixed while comparing the strongest practical complete workflows. It
estimates the effect of adopting the whole AI-assisted workflow. Component
replacements locate narrower contributions without pretending that interacting
parts make independent, additive contributions. Repeated runs and varied
conditions reveal whether the advantage survives changes in prompts, seeds,
workloads, designs, tools, and operating conditions. Healthy benchmarks keep
these comparisons readable through clear identity, representative tasks,
contamination controls, versioning, refresh, retirement, and reproducible
reporting.

Red teaming completes the evaluation. The candidate design and complete
workflow must face altered requirements, weakened checks, misleading feedback,
hidden behavior inserted into returned designs, triggered misbehavior in
workflow components, repeated-state loops, and failures of interruption and
recovery. The result is not a universal trust score. It is a qualified account
of where the design and workflow succeed, what they cost, what they depend on,
and how they fail.

The Lighthouse moonshot remains unresolved. The matched
complete-workflow comparison has not been run across the target
conditions and implementation checks. The resulting evaluation record can
inform an architecture commitment, but it does not authorize one. The remaining
question, taken up in @sec-what-architect-owns, is what architects contribute,
decide, and remain responsible for when the technical system can do substantial
work.
